author: Khen Elazar
title: My Hybrid Dividend Growth Strategy
text:
Introduction My main goal is to create real income using dividends. I am not necessarily looking for early retirement. I am more into the freedom that another source of income can deliver. Personally, I believe that the best way to achieve this goal is by investing in dividend paying stocks that tend to grow their annual payments. Therefore, I am using a dividend growth strategy.
Most of my portfolio is allocated towards this strategy. However, I know there are dozens of different strategies to create wealth. Some of them are riskier than my strategy. However, since I am investing for the long term, I allocate a small portion of my funds to them. I use them in order to achieve some additional returns. In the world of compounding interest every additional dollar can make a difference in the future.
I also have roughly 20% of my capital invested by investment house, which invests in stocks according to his discretion. I do it for the sake of diversification, and I also think that it's smart to have more than one person in charge of your investment strategy. I see it as a kind of a failsafe mechanism in case my dividend growth strategy fails.
In this article, I am going to share my strategy that is built mainly on dividend growth investing, but also utilizes other financial instruments and principals in order to create wealth. I am looking at stock options, free cash flow and some speculative stocks to create wealth.
Dividend growth investing This is my main strategy. I buy stocks on a monthly basis. I invest in companies that pay dividend and have a history of increasing the annual dividend payment. This way I can generate income that will grow together with the economy and with the earnings of the largest companies in the world. I have no intention to time the market and I invest every month whether the market is up or down.
I mitigate the risk of stocks by diversifying. I am diversified across different sectors. I own stocks in all ten sectors of the S&P 500. Within the sectors I also try to diversify and invest in a wide array of industries. This part of the strategy allows me to enjoy growth in every sector, and not be damaged to heavily if one sector lags or underperform.
Risk management is a key in my strategy, and since I understand the risk of holding individual stocks, I try to limit it. No stock should account for more than 5% of the portfolio or the income it generates. Right now, I have two companies that account for more than 5% of my dividend income, and I will not be adding to these positions anytime soon. It doesn’t necessarily say that they are bad investments, it means that I am more concerned with being too concentrated and not diversified. These stocks are Philip Morris ( PM ) and Omega Healthcare ( OHI ).
My goals in this strategy are set on an annual basis. I try to achieve meaningful dividend growth, and I do it by reinvesting my dividends and adding fresh funds to my portfolio. I am less concerned regarding my portfolio's performance compared to the S&P 500, and more concerned with the growth of my annual dividend income as this is my primary goals.
Free cash flow As a young investor, I have the time to wait for dividend growth machines to compound. Therefore, I am fine with investing in Visa ( V ) and Disney ( DIS ) who offer a very low yield, but high dividend growth rate. These companies offer immense cash flow, and very low payout ratios, so the companies still have plenty of room to grow their distributions quickly in the future.
It should be emphasized that dividends aren't magic that happens by itself. Dividends are born from free cash flow, and growing dividends are born from growing free cash flow. Since FCF is the base for dividends, I am fine with investing in companies that have growing FCF even if they don't pay dividends now.
These companies require even more patience from investors. I believe that eventually as they grow and become more mature, they will have to distribute some of their wealth in the form of dividends. The future dividend will probably be modest, but its growth should be impressive. This part of my strategy will only fit young dividend growth investors.
In this category I have Alphabet ( GOOG ) ( GOOGL ) and Facebook ( FB ). I hope that these two will follow Apple ( AAPL ) and Microsoft ( MSFT ). Both Apple and Microsoft enjoyed growing FCF, and at some point decided that the best way to share this growing FCF is by offering a dividend, and the dividend payment grew quickly since then.
Stock options I supplement my income by selling put options. When an investor sells a put option, he creates a contract with the buyer. The contract says that the seller is obligated to purchase the shares of specific company at a specific price. The buyer will exercise the contract if the price of the stock is lower than the execution price. As a seller I enjoy the premiums, and my risk is that I may be forced to buy stocks at a price which is higher than the market price.
I only use this strategy with companies I am willing to own. Let's assume that I see a company which trades at fair valuation, but I still don't feel comfortable enough buying it right now. I will sell put options with strike price which is 5%-10% lower. I will get the premium and use them to buy other stocks. If the price of the company hasn't changed or went up, I got the premiums. If the price went down, I will buy a company that I wanted to buy for a lower price. It's true that it may have reached an even lower price compared to the strike price, but if I bought a good company for a decent valuation, I am fine.
This way I see it as a win-win situation. I can either buy a stock that I want to own for a lower valuation compared to the current valuation or I don't buy the stock since its price went higher. Either way I get the premium which is real cash that supplement my dividend income and is used to buy more stocks that will generate more income.
Speculative stocks No more than 5% of my portfolio is devoted to these stocks. These are stocks that are very volatile and while they can offer immense returns under certain conditions the risks are massive. I invested in the highly leveraged B Communications ( BCOM ), and achieved triple digits returns several years ago. Right now, I own two companies that fit these criteria.
Speculative stocks can be found mainly in innovative industries such as biomed and information technology. While the share price can more than double itself, they may also be worth $0 if they fail to achieve their goals. They have very little margin of safety and should be monitored on a weekly basis. You should only invest in them if you can understand the underlying business.
These are the stocks you hear about from your friends at work, or that you read about, but not sure about them. Personally, it worked well for me, and while it didn’t make me rich, it did help me achieve some alpha. I find a candidate, read thoroughly about it, make sure I understand its business, and then consider investing a fraction of my portfolio in it.
Conclusion This is my strategy that served me well for over a decade. I am constantly trying to improve it. Try to think of ways to achieve additional income without increasing the risk levels significantly. Eventually the goal is to achieve the highest return with the lowest risk. While it sounds obvious any way that will allow me to lower my risk or increase my return will be considered.
I follow my dividend growth strategy, and most of my annual returns come from it. I use other strategies and instruments to supplement it, every investor should build his own strategy in a way that fits his risk appetite. You are more than welcome to adopt mine and ask any question you may have in the comments.
Disclosure: I am/we are long GOOG, APPL, FB, OHI, PM, V, DIS. I wrote this article myself, and it expresses my own opinions. I am not receiving compensation for it (other than from Seeking Alpha). I have no business relationship with any company whose stock is mentioned in this article.
